svg.title: Fabric Spark cluster architecture and the driver-to-executor 1:1 rule
svg.desc: A Fabric Spark pool is one head node running the driver's SparkContext, DAGScheduler, and Catalyst optimizer, plus worker nodes that each host exactly one executor JVM. This diagram shows the driver's internal coordination components, the fixed 1:1 node-to-executor ratio and its single-node pool exception, how a capacity SKU's vCore budget converts into a fixed count of executor slots, and the capacity-planning and failure-mode consequences of that fixed topology.
svg.text: Fabric Spark Cluster Architecture & the Driver-to-Executor 1:1 Rule
One head node runs the driver's coordination stack ➔ every remaining node hosts exactly one executor ➔ that fixed ratio is the unit capacity planning must reason in
ZONE 1 · POOL TOPOLOGY — ONE HEAD NODE, N WORKER NODES

g.title: Driver (head node) — hosts Livy, YARN Resource Manager, ZooKeeper, and the Spark driver process itself, which runs SparkContext, the DAGScheduler, the TaskScheduler, and the Catalyst optimizer.
g.text: One dedicated node — never runs task code
Entry point; registers the app with the
cluster manager and owns the session.
Cuts each job into stages at shuffle
task per output partition to a core.
plans every query, driver-side, before a task ships.
Session REST layer, resource manager, and
coordination service, co-located on this node.
One task scheduler → many executors: the driver is
a single process — it cannot be scaled out.

g.aria-label: Executors — one per worker node, fixed 1:1 ratio
g.title: Executors (worker nodes) — Fabric fixes the node-to-executor ratio at 1:1: one node is dedicated to the driver and each remaining node hosts exactly one executor JVM, which runs Node Agent and YARN Node Manager plus the Spark Executor service.
g.text: Exactly one Executor JVM per worker node
Node size chosen at pool creation = executor shape.
No per-node executor packing (unlike classic YARN).
between the pool's configured min and max nodes —
it never changes the 1:1 ratio itself.

g.title: Single-node pool exception — in a single-node pool, the driver and executor split that one node's resources roughly in half, a setup with restorable high availability aimed at small workloads, instead of a node being dedicated purely to the driver.
g.text: The one case where the 1:1 rule bends
Restorable HA, aimed at small workloads —
not a scaled-down version of the multi-node
topology; driver and executor now compete
Avoid for: sustained multi-job production load.

svg.text: ZONE 2 · WHY THE 1:1 RATIO IS THE CAPACITY-PLANNING UNIT

g.aria-label: SKU vCore budget converts to a fixed executor slot count
g.title: Capacity math — a Fabric capacity SKU sets a Spark vCore ceiling; custom pool node size sets vCores per node; because the ratio is fixed at 1:1, the vCore budget directly determines the maximum number of executor slots, not just a soft compute ceiling.

g.text: 8 GB RAM per vCore, fixed ratio
for the driver, off the top

svg.text: ZONE 3 · WHY THIS TOPOLOGY MATTERS FOR CAPACITY PLANNING

g.aria-label: Single driver becomes a coordination bottleneck
g.title: Single driver bottleneck — a single shared cluster funnels job submission and coordination through one driver node, which becomes a bottleneck under high job volume and can cause initialization failures when many jobs start together, because the driver is one unscalable process no matter how many executor nodes exist.
g.text: One shared cluster funnels ALL job
Under high job volume this becomes
a bottleneck, and many jobs starting
Adding executor nodes does not help —

g.title: Driver OOM from collect — calling df.toPandas() or summing values from df.collect() on the driver for a large DataFrame is the number-one cause of driver out-of-memory errors, since that single dedicated node has no executor-scale memory headroom; the fix is aggregating on executors and only ever collecting a small, deliberately bounded result.
g.text: Driver memory is not executor memory
DataFrame pulls the FULL result onto
Identified as the #1 cause of driver
has no distributed executor pool to

g.aria-label: Effective parallelism is capped at executor count
g.title: Effective parallelism ceiling — running many jobs on one shared cluster caps effective parallelism at the cluster's executor count, so a four-executor cluster behaves like four available execution slots regardless of how many jobs are queued; this is a direct, mechanical consequence of the fixed 1:1 ratio.

many jobs are queued behind it.

a pool IS sizing its concurrency: node
